narrative:
The model estimates a 68% chance that you will leave your job. In practical terms, that is high enough to treat you as a likely near-term leaver, so the promotion decision was denied: the organization is reluctant to award a promotion to someone it expects may soon depart.

The strongest reason is that you report having other job opportunities while in this role. Only about 23% of employees predicted to stay had that signal, so the model sees it as a clear pull toward leaving. Your tenure in your current organization—6–10 years—works in the opposite direction and is the second most influential factor; it acts as an anchor and modestly lowers the leave risk. Your total work experience of 6–10 years is the third most important factor and pushes the prediction back toward leaving, adding to the overall impression of mobility. Other profile details matter less than these three in this decision.

Given this, the useful next step is a frank retention and development conversation: clarify what would make you stay, whether the other opportunities are serious, and what promotion path and support could be committed over a defined period. If you intend to stay, make that concrete; if you are actively exploring outside options, the organization should address that openly before reconsidering promotion.
